analysis.one_liner: Suspends federal gasoline and diesel taxes for 90 days and opens the Arctic refuge to oil and gas drilling.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a House vote: introduced in May 2006 with 7 cosponsors, it was referred to two committees and died there when the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would do two things at once. For 90 days it would cut the federal tax on gasoline, diesel fuel, and kerosene to zero, meaning about 18 cents off every gallon at the pump — but it would repay the Highway Trust Fund out of general tax money so road funding stays whole. It would also permanently open the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's coastal plain to oil and gas leasing, ordering two lease sales by 2010 and writing rules that speed up the process and limit environmental review and court challenges. The bill died in committee without ever reaching the House floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers get roughly 18 cents per gallon off for 90 days (the bill text sets the tax rates to zero; the standard federal gasoline tax is 18.4 cents a gallon). Oil and gas companies gain access to lease, develop, and produce oil in the Arctic refuge's coastal plain — one of the largest untapped onshore oil areas in the United States.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers for 90 days; oil companies permanently

how_it_helps.text: Sets every federal tax rate on gasoline, diesel fuel, and kerosene to zero for the 90 days after enactment, lowering prices at the pump for that period.

Refunds dealers for fuel taxes already paid on inventory when the suspension starts, and refunds the Highway Trust Fund and the Leaking Underground Storage Tank Trust Fund for revenue lost during the suspension, so road and cleanup programs are not cut.

Authorizes oil and gas leasing in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coastal plain and directs the Interior Department to hold two lease sales before October 2010, requiring the government to collect fair market value for the public's minerals.

analysis.who_pays: General taxpayers — not just drivers — backfill the trust funds for the 90-day tax cut, since the bill treats the lost revenue as if it had been collected. The public also bears the permanent loss of protection for the Arctic refuge coastal plain, and the bill narrows the environmental review and court challenges that ordinary citizens could use to contest drilling.
analysis.who_pays_short: General taxpayers and the Arctic refuge

drawbacks.text: The 90-day tax holiday would cost the Treasury roughly what the fuel taxes raise — several billion dollars — and the bill repays the trust funds from general revenue, so non-drivers subsidize the pump discount and the savings per driver are modest (about 18 cents a gallon, roughly $25 for a typical driver over the period).

Nothing requires the tax cut to reach consumers: dealers get refunds on inventory and the savings at the pump depend on refiners and stations passing the cut along, which in a tight market they may not fully do.

The bill permanently opens the Arctic refuge coastal plain to drilling and stacks the process in favor of it: it declares drilling compatible with the refuge's purpose by fiat, deems a 1987 environmental statement sufficient, forbids studying a no-drilling alternative, allows only a 30-day public comment window, and channels all court challenges to a single appeals court with a 90-day deadline and narrow review.
Environmental damage to the refuge would be permanent; the bill's main protective limit is capping the surface footprint of production facilities at 2,000 acres.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer side is real but small and temporary — about 18 cents a gallon for 90 days, paid for out of the general Treasury rather than by cutting road funding. The drilling provision is the lasting part of the bill: it hands oil companies access to the Arctic refuge coastal plain permanently while cutting the environmental analysis, public comment, and judicial review that would otherwise apply. An honest reading is that a short-lived pump-price break is used to carry a long-term transfer of a public resource to the oil industry.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means and Natural Resources committees on the day it was introduced, got one routine request for Interior Department comment, and was never reported out or brought to the floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Marilyn Musgrave introduced the bill on May 23, 2006, during a spring of high gasoline prices, and it was referred the same day to the Ways and Means Committee (which handles taxes) and the Resources Committee (which handles public lands).
Seven Republican House members cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did.
On June 21, 2006, the House requested an executive comment from the Interior Department — a routine step — but neither committee ever took the bill up.
The bill received no committee vote, no floor vote, and no hearing action in the record, and expired when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the Arctic refuge coastal plain kept its protection from drilling, and general taxpayers were not asked to backfill the trust funds for a 90-day gas tax cut. Drivers did not get the temporary pump-price break they would otherwise have received.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Arctic refuge stayed protected; no taxpayer backfill

sides.party_line_note: All eight supporters in the record — the sponsor and her seven cosponsors — were Republicans, but the bill died in committee without any vote, so no opposition positions were ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would permanently open the Arctic refuge coastal plain to leasing and production, one of the largest untapped onshore oil areas in the U.S., while cutting the environmental review and legal avenues citizens could use to contest it. The industry's gain comes at the cost of permanently developing a protected public refuge.

A 90-day tax holiday gives dealers refunds on inventory and potentially higher margins if savings are not fully passed to drivers. Whether consumers get the full 18 cents per gallon depends entirely on market pass-through.

industries.industry: Road and bridge construction (Highway Trust Fund programs)
industries.note: The 90-day suspension would cut fuel tax receipts, but the bill reimburses the Highway Trust Fund in full from general revenue, so road funding continues. The cost simply shifts to all taxpayers, including those who do not drive.
